why: An essay built as one maxim with supports, four reasons and a set of test cases, so the lens leads with an argument tree. Hume's evidence is a tour of reported miracles across places and centuries, which a map and a timeline show faster than prose. His one numerical rule, 'deduct the smaller number from the greater', gets a small calculation so it can be compared with Laplace's and Venn's.

lenses.title: The maxim and its supports
lenses.why: The essay states a maxim (§91), argues for it in Part I and narrows it in Part II.

nodes.text: No testimony suffices for a miracle unless its falsehood would be more miraculous than the fact it reports (§91).
src: That no testimony is sufficient to establish a miracle, unless the testimony be of such a kind, that its falsehood would be more miraculous, than the fact, which it endeavours to establish

children.text: A wise man proportions belief to evidence; probability is a balance of opposed experiences (§87).
src: A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence.

children.text: Weigh the opposing experiments and subtract the smaller number from the greater.
src: In all cases, we must balance the opposite experiments, where they are opposite, and deduct the smaller number from the greater, in order to know the exact force of the superior evidence.

children.text: Trust in testimony itself rests only on experience that reports usually match facts (§88).
src: our assurance in any argument of this kind is derived from no other principle than our observation of the veracity of human testimony, and of the usual conformity of facts to the reports of witnesses.

children.text: An unusual fact sets one experience against another; only the surplus moves the mind (§89).
src: here is a contest of two opposite experiences; of which the one destroys the other, as far as its force goes, and the superior can only operate on the mind by the force, which remains.

children.text: The Roman proverb: 'I should not believe such a story were it told me by Cato'.
src: _I should not believe such a story were it told me by Cato_, was a proverbial saying in Rome

children.text: A miracle violates laws fixed by uniform experience, so the proof against it is as full as proof can be (§90).
src: A miracle is a violation of the laws of nature; and as a firm and unalterable experience has established these laws, the proof against a miracle, from the very nature of the fact, is as entire as any argument from experience can possibly be imagined.

children.text: Part II: in fact no miracle has ever been attested that well. Four reasons follow (§92).
src: it is easy to shew, that we have been a great deal too liberal in our concession, and that there never was a miraculous event established on so full an evidence.

children.text: 1. No miracle has enough witnesses of sense, integrity and reputation, testifying in public.
src: For _first_, there is not to be found, in all history, any miracle attested by a sufficient number of men, of such unquestioned good-sense, education, and learning, as to secure us against all delusion in themselves

children.text: 2. Surprise and wonder are pleasant, so they incline us to believe (§93).
src: The passion of _surprise_ and _wonder_, arising from miracles, being an agreeable emotion, gives a sensible tendency towards the belief of those events, from which it is derived.

children.text: Rumours of marriages spread fastest in country towns.
src: There is no kind of report which rises so easily, and spreads so quickly, especially in country places and provincial towns, as those concerning marriages

children.text: 3. Miracle stories abound among 'ignorant and barbarous nations' (§94).
src: It forms a strong presumption against all supernatural and miraculous relations, that they are observed chiefly to abound among ignorant and barbarous nations

children.text: Alexander the false prophet started in Paphlagonia; only a passing Lucian exposed him.
src: It was a wise policy in that false prophet, Alexander, who though now forgotten, was once so famous, to lay the first scene of his impostures in Paphlagonia

children.text: 4. Rival religions' miracles discredit one another, so the testimony destroys itself (§95).
src: so that not only the miracle destroys the credit of testimony, but the testimony destroys itself.

children.text: Like a judge weighing two witnesses to a crime against two who place the accused far away.
src: the reasoning of a judge, who supposes, that the credit of two witnesses, maintaining a crime against any one, is destroyed by the testimony of two others, who affirm him to have been two hundred leagues distant

children.text: Some miracles are very well attested: Vespasian at Alexandria, the door-keeper of Saragossa, the tomb of the Abbé Paris (§96).
src: One of the best attested miracles in all profane history, is that which Tacitus reports of Vespasian

children.text: Against a 'cloud of witnesses' Hume sets only the impossibility of the events, and holds that this suffices.
src: And what have we to oppose to such a cloud of witnesses, but the absolute impossibility or miraculous nature of the events, which they relate? And this surely, in the eyes of all reasonable people, will alone be regarded as a sufficient refutation.

children.text: Conclusion: testimony for a miracle never reaches even probability; the subtraction leaves nothing (§98).
src: no testimony for any kind of miracle has ever amounted to a probability, much less to a proof
this substraction, with regard to all popular religions, amounts to an entire annihilation

children.text: The limit: a miracle might be proved by testimony, but never as the foundation of a religion (§99).
src: I beg the limitations here made may be remarked, when I say, that a miracle can never be proved, so as to be the foundation of a system of religion.

children.text: So religion rests on faith, not reason: believing it is itself 'a continued miracle' (§100–101).
src: Our most holy religion is founded on _Faith_, not on reason
is conscious of a continued miracle in his own person, which subverts all the principles of his understanding

lenses.title: Cases at the edge of the maxim
lenses.why: Hume tests his own rule on cases that should, and should not, be believed.

cases.rule: Reject testimony that runs against all of one's experience.
ruleSrc: The Indian prince, who refused to believe the first relations concerning the effects of frost, reasoned justly
cases.case: Frost is real. Hume answers that it was outside the prince's experience, not against it: extraordinary, not miraculous.
src: Though they were not contrary to his experience, they were not conformable to it.
Such an event, therefore, may be denominated _extraordinary_, and requires a pretty strong testimony, to render it credible to people in a warm climate: But still it is not _miraculous_

cases.rule: No human testimony can prove a miracle (the maxim of §98).
ruleSrc: we may establish it as a maxim, that no human testimony can have such force as to prove a miracle
cases.case: If every author in every language reported eight days of total darkness from 1 January 1600, philosophers should accept it and look for causes.
src: suppose, all authors, in all languages, agree, that, from the first of January 1600, there was a total darkness over the whole earth for eight days
it is evident, that our present philosophers, instead of doubting the fact, ought to receive it as certain, and ought to search for the causes whence it might be derived.

cases.rule: Testimony that is extensive and uniform enough can establish an event with analogies in nature, like the darkness.
ruleSrc: any phenomenon, which seems to have a tendency towards that catastrophe, comes within the reach of human testimony, if that testimony be very extensive and uniform.
cases.case: Equally uniform testimony that Queen Elizabeth died and reigned again three years later would not move him: knavery and folly are commoner than resurrection.
src: I must confess that I should be surprised at the concurrence of so many odd circumstances, but should not have the least inclination to believe so miraculous an event.

the knavery and folly of men are such common phenomena, that I should rather believe the most extraordinary events to arise from their concurrence, than admit of so signal a violation of the laws of nature.

lenses.title: Hume's balance of experiments
lenses.why: Hume's only quantitative rule. He gives two cases and no formula, so the second line is the annotator's frequency reading, for comparison with Laplace and Venn.
src: A hundred instances or experiments on one side, and fifty on another, afford a doubtful expectation of any event; though a hundred uniform experiments, with only one that is contradictory, reasonably beget a pretty strong degree of assurance.

params.label: Experiments on one side
src: A hundred instances or experiments on one side

params.label: Experiments on the other
src: and fifty on another, afford a doubtful expectation of any event

steps.label: Hume: deduct the smaller number from the greater
src: deduct the smaller number from the greater, in order to know the exact force of the superior evidence.

steps.label: Annotator: share of experience on the stronger side
src: All probability, then, supposes an opposition of experiments and observations, where the one side is found to overbalance the other, and to produce a degree of evidence, proportioned to the superiority.
steps.note: Hume's 'doubtful' case (100 to 50) gives 2/3; his 'pretty strong' case (100 to 1) gives 100/101. Venn (ch. XVII §13–14) denies that any such rule has general value.

plot.caption: Share on the stronger side as contrary experiments accumulate (annotator's reading).

lenses.title: Hume's working vocabulary
lenses.why: 'Proof' and 'probability' are technical terms here, and the French cases bring their own vocabulary.

terms.period: An argument from experience that has been uniform, stronger than probability.
terms.modern: Near-certainty from an exceptionless record; not a deductive proof.
src: regards his past experience as a full _proof_ of the future existence of that event.

terms.period: Evidence where experiences conflict and one side outweighs the other.
src: All probability, then, supposes an opposition of experiments and observations

terms.period: The doctrine that Christ's body is present in the Eucharist.
src: an argument against the _real presence_

terms.modern: A wonder, an anomaly taken as a sign.
src: For so long, I presume, will the accounts of miracles and prodigies be found in all history, sacred and profane.
who refused to believe the first relations concerning the effects of frost

terms.period: A friar of the Capuchin order, a popular preacher.
src: every _Capuchin_, every itinerant or stationary teacher can perform over the generality of mankind

terms.period: Rival Catholic parties in France: Augustinian rigorists against the Jesuit-backed followers of Molina.

src: The Molinist party had tried to discredit these miracles in one instance

terms.period: A bishop's court (Hume glosses it himself).
src: the officiality or bishop's court at Paris

terms.period: A phrase from Lucretius: the race greedy for ears.
terms.modern: People eager to hear and repeat stories.
src: The _avidum genus auricularum_[25], the gazing populace, receive greedily, without examination, whatever sooths superstition, and promotes wonder.
